title: Burning a name on a wooden spoon
subtitle: Personalising a kitchen utensil with pyrography lettering
excerpt: A personalised wooden spoon with a name or initial burned into the handle. The handle of a standard wooden spoon is the ideal size for a short word in block capitals or a simple script initial. A practical first project that makes a useful gift.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from established British pyrography workshop teaching; personalised wooden spoon as beginner project documented in UK craft magazines and craft fair traditions.

glossaryTerms.definition: The craft of decorating wood by burning designs onto the surface with a heated metal tip.

content.text: A wooden spoon with a name burned into the handle: a first
pyrography

project that produces something useful and personal. A standard kitchen spoon handle is 12 to 15 cm long and 25 to 30 mm wide. There is room for a five- or six-letter name in block capitals, or a large decorative initial. The spoon is unfinished; the pyrography is the finish.
Before you start burning.
Hot tip: a pyrography burner tip reaches 200 to 400 degrees C. Never touch the tip or rest it face-down on any surface. Use the stand between every stroke.
Fumes: burning wood produces fine particles. Work near an open window with a small fan behind you.
Treated wood: only burn plain, unfinished timber. Do not burn painted, varnished, or oiled spoons.
The spoon

Use a plain, unfinished wooden spoon in beech, sycamore, or lime. Many craft suppliers sell blank spoons ready for decoration. Avoid spoons sold in supermarkets or kitchen shops; these are often finished with food-safe oil or lacquer, which burns badly and releases fumes. Check by wiping the handle with a damp cloth: if a light sheen comes off, the spoon has a surface coating. Source an unfinished blank instead.
Preparing the surface

Fold a piece of 240-grit paper in half and lightly sand the flat back face of the handle. Two or three passes is enough. This removes any surface oils from handling and opens the grain for a cleaner burn. Wipe the dust off with a dry cloth.
Laying out the letters

Draw a faint pencil centre line along the length of the handle. Mark the centre of the name on that line, then space the letters outward. For block capitals, each letter is about 8 to 10 mm tall and 6 to 8 mm wide, with 3 mm between letters. For a single initial, use the full handle width: a letter 20 mm tall fits a 25 mm wide handle with a small margin. Keep the pencil marks very light; they burn the same colour as the design if they are heavy.
Burning the letters

Set the burner to medium heat and test on a piece of scrap timber of the same species. Each stroke burns one straight or curved element. For block capitals, work each letter from top to bottom, left to right. Verticals first, then horizontals, then diagonals. Keep the tip moving at a consistent speed; pausing burns a darker spot. Round letters (C, O, G, S) use a single slow arc stroke for each curve.
Finishing after burning

Do not oil or finish the spoon after burning. A food-safe finish on a pyrography piece is not necessary; the burned surface is stable and hardened. If the spoon will be used for stirring (not just display), wipe the bowl and shaft only with a little walnut oil or raw linseed oil. Keep the handle dry; oils darken the surrounding wood and can obscure the lettering over time.
Variations
Script initial: a large cursive letter fills the whole handle. It is more forgiving of minor wobbles than a full name in block capitals.
Date: add a wedding date or birth year below the name in smaller numerals. Two rows on a wide handle, or a single row on a narrow one.
Simple motif border: a row of small dashes or dots framing the name. Burn at low heat. No pattern-drawing skills needed.

attrs.symptom: The letters are uneven in size
attrs.cause: The pencil guide marks were not ruled carefully before burning.
attrs.fix: Rule two parallel lines as height guides before sketching the letters. Remove with an eraser after burning.

attrs.symptom: The burn is dark brown in some strokes and pale in others
attrs.cause: Inconsistent speed: pausing makes dark spots, moving fast makes pale lines.
attrs.fix: Practise on scrap timber at a constant speed. One smooth pull stroke per element is better than multiple hesitant passes.
